hints: Work backwards from step 3. The product of step 3 has a $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{Br}$ side chain on the right hand ring, so what alkyl side chain in T could give that by side chain bromination?
Work backwards from ketoprofen. Step 5 converts U into $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, so what functional group hydrolyses on heating with aqueous acid to give a carboxylic acid?
walkthrough:
Read the carbon skeleton that never changes**
Look along the whole scheme. The left hand $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4$ benzophenone unit stays intact from step 1 right through to ketoprofen. Only the side chain on the right hand ring changes. So T and U must both contain that same benzoyl phenyl core.

Deduce T by looking forward to the bromide**
Step 3 gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{Br}$. That is a benzylic bromide made by free radical substitution of a benzylic C-H by Br. The precursor must therefore be the ethyl compound $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. This also fits the formula $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$. That is T.

Deduce U by looking forward to the acid**
Ketoprofen has $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Step 5 must be hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid. So U must be the nitrile $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CN}$, formed from the bromide in step 4 by $\text{CN}^-$ substitution.

Final answer: T is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (3-ethylbenzophenone skeleton, ethyl group meta to the carbonyl).
U is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CN}$ (Br replaced by CN, same carbon skeleton).

hints: Step 1 forms benzophenone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_5$ from benzene. Which acyl chloride plus $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst introduces a $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}$ group?
Step 2 adds an ethyl group to the ring. Which chloroalkane plus $\text{AlCl}_3$ introduces a $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group?
Step 3 converts benzylic $\text{CH}_2$ to benzylic $\text{CHBr}$. What reagent gives free radical substitution at the side chain rather than the ring?
Step 4 converts $\text{RBr}$ to $\text{RCN}$. Which source of $\text{CN}^-$ is used, and in which solvent to favour substitution?
Step 5 converts $\text{RCN}$ to $\text{RCO}_2\text{H}$. What aqueous reagent and heating condition hydrolyses a nitrile fully to the acid?
walkthrough:
Step 1, acylation to benzophenone**
Benzene to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_5$ is Friedel-Crafts acylation. You need to supply the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C=O}$ electrophile. Use benzoyl chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$, with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst and heat. The $\text{AlCl}_3$ generates the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}^+\text{=O}$ electrophile.

Step 2, alkylation to introduce ethyl**
Benzophenone to T adds $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to the second ring. This is Friedel-Crafts alkylation. Use chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ and heat to generate the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ electrophile.

Step 3, benzylic bromination**
T to the benzylic bromide is free radical substitution of the side chain, not electrophilic bromination of the ring. The ketone deactivates the rings, and light directs attack to the benzylic position. Use $\text{Br}_2$ with uv light (or strong heat). No $\text{FeBr}_3$ or $\text{AlBr}_3$ carrier, otherwise you would brominate the ring.

Step 4, forming the nitrile**
Alkyl bromide to alkyl nitrile is nucleophilic substitution by cyanide. Use $\text{KCN}$ (or $\text{NaCN}$) warmed in ethanol. Ethanolic conditions are important to dissolve the organic bromide and favour substitution over hydrolysis.

Step 5, hydrolysis to ketoprofen**
Nitrile U to carboxylic acid is acid hydrolysis. Boil / heat under reflux with aqueous acid such as $\text{HCl(aq)}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{aq})$, written as $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. Heat is essential because hydrolysis of $\text{RCN}$ via the amide to the acid needs prolonged strong heating.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} + \text{AlCl}_3$, heat
step 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3$, heat
step 3: $\text{Br}_2$, uv light (or heat)
step 4: $\text{KCN}$ (or $\text{NaCN}$), heat in ethanol (or ethanolic)
step 5: $\text{H}^+ (\text{aq})$ / $\text{HCl(aq)}$ / $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{aq})$, heat / boil / reflux

hints: In step 1 benzene attacks an electrophile generated from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$ and $\text{AlCl}_3$, keeping the aromatic ring. What is the general name for attack on a benzene ring?

In step 5 a nitrile $\text{CN}$ group is cleaved by water / aqueous acid to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. What is the general name for splitting by water, and what is happening at carbon in terms of nucleophile?
walkthrough:
Classify step 1**
Think of what attacks what. In step 1 the benzene pi system attacks the acylium electrophile, then $\text{H}^+$ is lost and aromaticity is restored. A hydrogen on the ring is substituted by an electrophile, so this is electrophilic substitution.

Classify step 5**
Think of what water does. In step 5 water (under acid catalysis) adds across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ bond and cleaves it to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ plus $\text{NH}_4^+$. Breaking a molecule using water is hydrolysis. At the nitrile carbon, water acts as a nucleophile, so nucleophilic substitution is also accepted.

Final answer: step 1: electrophilic substitution (Friedel-Crafts acylation)
step 5: hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution / acid hydrolysis)
